summary: Specifies the syntax and processing rules for XML digital signatures. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A signature on a paper proves who wrote it. This is the way to put such a proof on a web-style data file.

questions: what is signedinfo in xml signature
subtitle: The XML syntax and processing rules for signing any data, built around a Signature element that digests and signs references.

tldr.problem: Applications needed a standard way to attach integrity, message authentication and signer authentication to data of any type, whether the data sits inside the XML document or elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: A Signature element holds a SignedInfo block listing each signed item with its transforms, digest method and digest value. SignedInfo is canonicalized and signed, and an optional KeyInfo tells the recipient which key to use.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 3075. It does not say how keys relate to people, so applications must supply their own trust decisions.

today: RFC 3275 is a Draft Standard published in March 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 3075.

sections.title: What XML Signatures Do and Do Not Do
sections.content:
This RFC specifies XML syntax and processing rules for creating and representing digital signatures. A signature can cover any digital content, including XML. Enveloped or enveloping signatures are over data within the same XML document as the signature. Detached signatures are over data external to the Signature element.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The XML Signature is a method of associating a key with referenced data (octets). It does not say how keys are associated with persons or institutions, nor what the signed data means. An application built on it must add its own key, algorithm, processing and rendering requirements.

There is no explicit version number. A future version would use a different namespace, and implementations of this specification MUST use http://www.w3.org/2000/09/xmldsig#. The schema definition is normative. The RFC states that the corresponding W3C Recommendation is dated 2002-02-12 in its URL.
sections.eli5: It is a stamp-making kit for data files. It tells you how to make the stamp, but not who is allowed to own one.

sections.title: The Signature Structure
sections.content:
Data objects are signed through an indirection. Each object is digested, the digest goes into a Reference element, and the block of references is itself canonicalized and signed. The root is the Signature element, containing in order SignedInfo, SignatureValue, an optional KeyInfo and zero or more Object elements.

SignedInfo is what is actually signed. It holds a CanonicalizationMethod, a SignatureMethod and one or more Reference elements. The algorithm names are inside the signed part so that an attacker cannot substitute a weaker algorithm. Each Reference has an optional URI naming the data object, optional Transforms, a DigestMethod and a DigestValue.

The URI may be omitted on at most one Reference. The verifier may obtain the content from somewhere other than the URI, such as a local store, as long as the digest verifies. KeyInfo is optional because the signer may not want to reveal key information, or the application context may already identify the key. Since it sits outside SignedInfo, a Reference can be added to bind it to the signature.
sections.eli5: You write a list of things you are signing and a fingerprint of each one. Then you sign the whole list once.

sections.title: Generating and Validating Signatures
sections.content:
Core generation has two parts. For each data object, apply the Transforms, calculate the digest, and create a Reference. Then create SignedInfo, canonicalize it, and calculate the SignatureValue over it using the algorithms named inside.

Core validation has two required steps. Reference validation canonicalizes SignedInfo, then for each Reference obtains the data object, digests it with the stated DigestMethod and compares the result to the stated DigestValue. Any mismatch fails validation. Signature validation obtains the key from KeyInfo or an outside source and confirms the SignatureValue over the canonical SignedInfo.

Comparisons are made over the numeric or decoded octet values, not the encoded text, so accidental white space in the encoding does not matter. The RFC also warns that a valid signature may be one a given application cannot validate, for example because it does not implement an optional part or will not dereference a certain URI scheme.
sections.eli5: To check a signature, you redo the fingerprints yourself and see if they match. If even one is different, the signature fails.

sections.title: References, Transforms and URIs
sections.content:
A Reference's URI identifies the data object. Applications MUST be able to parse URI syntax and RECOMMENDED to dereference HTTP URIs. An external resource must come back as an octet stream. An XML document is only parsed if the URI is a same-document reference or a transform needs parsed XML. The null URI URI="" selects every non-comment node of the containing document. A fragment like #chapter1 selects that element and its descendants, without comments.

The optional Transforms element is an ordered list. The output of each is the input of the next, and the last one feeds the digest. The signer therefore signs the transformed data, not the original. Data is either an octet stream or an XPath node-set, and the default is to parse octets into a node-set, or to turn a node-set into octets with Canonical XML, when the next step needs the other form.

The standard transforms are canonicalization, base64 decoding, XPath filtering, the enveloped signature transform and XSLT. The enveloped signature transform removes the Signature element containing it from the digest, which a signature inside the content it signs needs. The Type attribute on a Reference is advisory and core behavior does not check it.
sections.eli5: Before fingerprinting, you may first tidy or cut the data in agreed steps, such as leaving out the signature itself. Anyone checking must follow the same steps.

sections.title: KeyInfo and Key Types
sections.content:
KeyInfo helps the recipient find the validation key. It may hold keys, names, certificates and other key management data. Questions of trust in that information, such as its authenticity or strength, are out of scope. Compliant versions MUST implement KeyValue and SHOULD implement RetrievalMethod.

The defined children are KeyName (a string key identifier), KeyValue (a single public key, with DSA required and RSA recommended), RetrievalMethod (a pointer to key data stored elsewhere), X509Data (certificates, issuer and serial pairs, subject names, key identifiers or revocation lists), PGPData, SPKIData and MgmtData.

Big integers such as RSA moduli use the ds:CryptoBinary type: a big-endian integer without leading zero octets, then base64 encoded. An RSA key has a Modulus and an Exponent. A DSA key has fields P, Q, G, Y, J, Seed and PgenCounter, several optional.
sections.eli5: KeyInfo is a note saying which key opens this lock. It can carry the key, a name for it, or directions to where it is kept.

sections.title: Algorithms and Extra Elements
sections.content:
Algorithms are named by URIs. The RFC sets implementation requirements, not usage requirements, and allows other algorithms.

  • Digest: SHA-1 is required. MD5 is NOT RECOMMENDED because recent cryptanalysis cast doubt on its strength.
  • MAC: HMAC-SHA1 is required.
  • Signature: DSA with SHA-1 is required and RSA with SHA-1 is recommended.
  • Canonicalization: Canonical XML, which omits comments, is required. Canonical XML with Comments is recommended.
  • Encoding: base64 is required.
  • Transforms: the enveloped signature is required, XPath is recommended and XSLT is optional.

The optional Object element carries any data inside the signature and is typically used for enveloping signatures. The optional Manifest is a list of References whose digests the application, not core validation, decides whether to check. This allows partial success, or one set of references shared by several signatures. SignatureProperties holds facts about the signing, such as a time stamp. Canonicalization matters because signatures only work if verification runs over exactly the same bits as signing.
sections.eli5: The RFC picks one standard set of tools that every program must have, so two programs can always understand each other's signatures.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several cautions. Because of transforms, only what is signed is secure: information discarded by a transform is not protected, and an envelope around signed data is not secured by the signature. Core validation also does not confirm that the digested data was really obtained by applying the transforms.

A signer should sign only what the user "sees", and a verifier should work from the transformed, signed data and not the original. For example, an external style sheet should be signed through a Reference, or it could change the result without invalidating the signature. Documents handled by signature applications MUST be in Unicode normalization form NFC.

An arbitrary CanonicalizationMethod is dangerous. Since it sits inside SignedInfo, it could rewrite URIs or even erase itself from the canonical form, making the signature meaningless.

Public key signatures and keyed hash codes have different models. With a shared secret key, any verifier can forge signatures. Overall strength depends on every link, including key generation, key size, certificate validation and care in running algorithms or XSLT with hostile parameters.
sections.eli5: A signature only protects what was really signed, so check what you signed. Also a fake rule for tidying the data could make a bad file look fine.
